oneSentence: A single row of training data used to adjust a model, often made of input values and, in some methods, a target answer.
plainExplanation:
A training example is one item a machine-learning system learns from. It might be one row in a table, one image, one short text, one sound clip, or one event in a log. A collection of these items is a dataset, but each individual item is a training example.

People also say sample or instance. In many introductions, these words are used almost interchangeably for one item in the data. But they can carry slightly different emphasis. Sample often points to something taken from a larger population, while instance often means one concrete case represented in the model's input format.

What goes in depends on the learning method. In supervised learning, one example usually contains input features, meaning the measurable parts the model receives, plus a label, meaning the target answer. In unsupervised learning, an example may have only the input features. During training, the system processes many examples and may update internal numbers so later it can produce predictions for new cases.

What comes out is a trained system. In many methods, this is a changed model rather than a stored answer for each example. A single example usually changes the model only a little. After many examples, patterns in the data can shape how the model behaves. This term is often confused with feature, which is one column or property inside an example, and with dataset, which is the full collection of examples.

everydayAnalogy.title: Learning the pastry counter
everydayAnalogy.story: A new bakery assistant learns the products by seeing one item at a time together with its correct name. One round pastry, shown with the label "bagel", is a single example. Its shape and appearance are the input, and the name is the target answer. The assistant needs many varied examples before reliably recognising new items. Likewise, one training example contributes to learning, but does not establish the whole pattern by itself.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: Real machine-learning examples are usually turned into numeric representations before the model can use them, while the card story stays human-readable. Also, not every training example has a known correct answer: in unsupervised or self-supervised learning, the system may learn from structure in the inputs rather than from a back-of-card label.

visual.title: From one example to a trained model
visual.learningObjective: Show that one training example is a single learning item, and many such items gradually change a model during training.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram. It starts with one example shown as a single row, then zooms out to many rows, then shows repeated passes through a model, and ends with an updated model used on new input. Read from left to right to see how one item differs from the full collection and how repeated examples affect training.

steps.label: One item
steps.explanation: Show a single example as one row: input text or values, and, if available, the target answer.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw one rectangular card split into two sections labelled Input and Target. Add a note below: 'One training example'.

steps.label: Many items
steps.explanation: Training usually uses many examples together, not just one.
steps.visualInstruction: Duplicate the card into a stacked set of rows. Label the stack 'Training data: many examples'.

steps.label: Model update
steps.explanation: Each example contributes a small update to the model's internal numbers during training.
steps.visualInstruction: Connect the stack to a central model box with looping arrows. Add small gear or slider icons and a label: 'Adjust internal parameters a little at a time'.

steps.label: After training
steps.explanation: The result is an updated model that can take new input and produce a prediction.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a second model box on the right labelled 'Trained model', with one new input card going in and one prediction card coming out.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each stage to highlight the difference between one example, the collection of examples, and the trained model produced after repeated updates.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram explains that a training example is one individual learning item, not the whole dataset and not the model itself. First, it shows one row containing an input and, where relevant, a target answer. Next, it shows many such rows grouped together as training data. Then arrows lead to a model box, with loops indicating repeated updates from many examples. Finally, a trained model receives a new input and outputs a prediction. The message is that one example is a single case, many examples are used during training, and the output of training is an updated model.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-panel diagram shows: one example, many examples, repeated model updates, and a trained model making a prediction on new input. No animation is used; the loops are shown as fixed arrows.

workedExample.scenario: For the audit file, the desk officer shows how one reviewed request contributes to training a classifier that routes messages as either programme or administration.
workedExample.input: One example: subject line = "Comments requested on draft workplan"; reviewed target = "programme"
process: Convert the permitted words or other attributes into an input vector, conventionally written as x.
Pair that vector with the reviewed target y, in this case "programme".
Have the current model calculate its predicted category or category probabilities.
Compare the prediction with the target and calculate the error for this example.
Use that error, alone or combined with errors from a batch, to adjust the model's parameters slightly.
workedExample.result: The example does not create a fixed rule that every message mentioning a workplan is programme-related. It contributes a small adjustment alongside many other examples, from which the model learns broader statistical patterns.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A desk officer in a Resident Coordinator's Office is closing an internal audit query about a classifier that routes incoming requests to the correct focal point. The file needs a concrete account of the training data. One training example is one previously reviewed request, represented by permitted text features, paired with the routing category assigned by staff.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The example may be processed alone or in a batch. Its features and reviewed target help determine a small parameter adjustment. The audit response can therefore distinguish one training example from the full dataset, which is a useful distinction when the annex is due by close of business.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Requests may contain names, contact details or confidential material. They must not be copied into a tool that has not been approved for that information. Use only necessary fields, follow the office's data protection guidance, restrict access and retain human review of routing decisions.

whyItMatters: If you can recognise what counts as one training example, you can ask better questions about quality, bias, coverage and privacy. For example: does each example represent a real case, is the label trustworthy, are important groups missing, and is one person or event counted many times? These questions affect whether a system learns useful patterns or misleading ones. The term also helps you separate three different things that are often mixed up: one example, the full dataset, and the trained model.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A training example is the same as the whole dataset.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A dataset is the collection. A training example is one item inside it, such as one row, one image or one text. Confusing the two makes it harder to judge how much data a model actually learned from and whether the data covers enough cases.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A training example always includes the correct answer.
commonMisconceptions.correction: That is true in many supervised-learning setups, where an example has inputs and a label. But in unsupervised, self-supervised and some other methods, examples may not have a human-provided target answer. The system may instead learn patterns, structure or useful representations from the inputs themselves.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: One example teaches the model a complete rule.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Usually one example only causes a small update. Models typically need many examples because they are estimating patterns across data, not copying a single case into a reliable general rule. If one example has too much influence, that can be a sign of overfitting or data imbalance.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A training example is one piece of data the system learns from, like one row in a spreadsheet or one labelled image.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Technically, a training example is one observation used by a learning algorithm. In optimisation-based methods, it is often represented as an input vector x and, in supervised learning, an associated target y. The terms sample and instance are often used for the same unit, though sample may emphasise that the observation was drawn from a broader population, and instance may emphasise one concrete case in feature space. Examples may be processed singly or in batches, and each can contribute to an update of model parameters. The usual result is an adjusted model, not a permanent one-to-one lookup table of the examples.

keyTakeaway: A training example is one observation presented to the learning process, often as input x paired with target y. It can influence the model alone or as part of a batch.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes a training example?
options: The entire collection of data used to build a model
One individual case used during learning, such as one row, image or text item
A single feature, such as age or document length
The model's final answer for a new case
quickCheck.explanation: A training example is one case in the data. The whole collection is the dataset, a feature is one property inside an example, and the model's final answer on new input is a prediction.

issues.problem: The definition calls every training example a "row", but the page later correctly includes images, text, sound clips and events. This wording unnecessarily narrows the term and conflicts with the broader explanation.
issues.fix: A single item of training data used to adjust a model, often made of input values and, in some methods, a target answer.

issues.problem: The explanation presents parameter updates and the absence of stored examples as universal. Some learning methods do not train by repeatedly updating internal numbers, and a trained system can retain training examples rather than only producing a changed parameterised model.

issues.problem: "Each example contributes a small update" implies that every example causes an individual update of a reliably small size. The page's technical section correctly says examples may be processed in batches, so an update may combine several examples. Update size is also not guaranteed to be small.
issues.fix: Examples contribute information used to adjust the model's internal numbers during training.

issues.problem: The example contains the word "Flight", but not "hotels" or "itineraries". With the stated word-presence features, this example cannot directly increase the influence of those absent words. No arithmetic is present in the worked example, so there is no numerical calculation to verify.
issues.fix: This single example does not create a rule by itself, but it can nudge the model so future subject lines containing similar learned features, such as "flight", are more likely to be classified as travel.
